newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: CA privatisation focus at Austria crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: CA privatisation focus at Austria crisis talks.

text.p: Austria's two-party coalition government met in crisis session on Saturday to air opposing views on the sale of flagship bank, Creditanstalt, before Finance Minister Viktor Klima announces a winning bid.

The sale of the government's 70 percent voting stake in 141-year-old Creditanstalt has whipped up a political storm and threatens to derail the fragile alliance of dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party.

Klima, a Social Democrat, said he would reveal the winner of the seven-year fight for control of Creditanstalt before Tuesday, when parliament is due to hold a special session on the politically contentious sale.
Leaders of the two parties looked set for a long haul to try to end the government crisis as talks dragged on into Saturday evening.
"We will continue the talks tonight, we will continue the talks tomorrow, we will continue day and night," a source close to the talks told reporters.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats want Creditanstalt to be sold to Bank Austria.

But the conservatives say a sale to Bank Austria would not be a genuine privatisation because the bank is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-ruled City of Vienna through its Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation.

AVZ directly owns around 46 percent of Bank Austria voting shares and also guarantees the bank's liabilities. The conservatives have said it could only foresee a sale to Bank Austria if the City of Vienna withdrew fully from Bank Austria.
Credit rating agencies have said such a withdrawal would prove extremely costly for Bank Austria as it would then lose its AAA rating.

The conservatives, backed by Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party, also want to ensure Creditanstalt's small shareholders receive the same price per share as the 861 schillings Bank Austria has offered.

This may also prove too dear for the Alpine republic's banking giant when compared to Friday's close of 720.5 schillings. Experts say Bank Austria may consider the takeover of Creditanstalt is coming at too high a cost.

The People's Party, together with Creditanstalt's management, favour an international consortium led by insurer EA-Generali. The unfancied third bid comes from a foundation owned by retail magnate Karl Wlaschek.
The finance minister's deadline for improved bids from the three bidders expired on Friday, when both Bank Austria and the consortium topped up their original offers.
Klima has repeatedly stressed that he is bound by Austrian and European Union law to sell the state's stake of 19.9 million ordinary voting shares to the highest offer.
Bank Austria remains the frontrunner after it raised its offer to 17.1 billion schillings from 16.7 billion, state television said on Saturday.
The EA-Generali consortium also raised its bid but trails far behind Bank Austria at 14.3 billion schillings. The group originally bid 13.8 billion.
No one in the Finance Ministry was immediately available to confirm the figures.
Wlaschek has stuck to his initial offer of 12 billion schillings, television said.
